title.narrative: OP 2.1: CBOs from south and west Mosul are selected and capacitated on mediation, negotiation, advocacy and on the early warning mechanisms; and providing early warning signals to prevent violent extremism.

description.narrative: A significant step was achieved by developing a transparent evaluation mechanism, complete with specific criteria, to select the Community-Based Organisations (CBOs) participating in the project from a pool of 18 organisations that participated in the previous project. In total, six CBOs were chosen based on their primary focus on supporting youth and women, thereby representing the targeted areas of the project. The evaluation process drew upon reports from the M&E Department, evaluations by recipients of the previous project, and feedback from beneficiaries of its activities. This comprehensive approach ensured a thorough assessment of each CBO's suitability for participation in the current project.The selected CBOs participated in a comprehensive orientation session conducted by TAD about the new project and signed collaboration agreements with the six chosen organisations. Following this, TAD launched a series of capacity-building workshops on mediation, negotiation, and advocacy. Participants then shared the knowledge gained with their respective staff to ensure widespread understanding and implementation.TAD has provided institutional capacity development packages for the six CBOs through coaching and mentoring the CBOs’ staff in media, finance, HR, and procurement departments, leading to improved documentation and communication of their activities, enhanced financial transparency and procurement processes, and increased visibility and engagement within the community.

title.narrative: Number of CBOs’ staff attended training courses on mediation, negotiation, advocacy and warning mechanisms (desegregated by subject and female/ male).

description.narrative: TAD invited 18 participants, with three from each CBO (nine men and nine women), to be trained in mediation, negotiation, advocacy, and early warning mechanisms. An experienced external trainer was hired to develop a training manual and conduct a three-day workshop. The trainer not only enhanced participants' knowledge but also assisted them in passing on the training to their colleagues. In August, TAD began the capacity development for the six CBOs. TAD has developed their capacity institutionally by providing coaching and mentoring in media, finance, HR, and procurement. The media training, attended by six participants (one from each CBO, one woman and five men), provided their media and communication focal points/teams with essential skills in media coverage, photography, videography, news writing, and content creation. This training enabled them to document activities more effectively, create engaging content, and raise awareness about the issues they advocate for. Media officers were nominated to ensure the consistent application of these skills. The finance management, HR, and procurement training, attended by 13 participants (seven women and six men), focused on budgeting, expenditure tracking, and procurement processes, providing detailed guidance on contract terms and financial documentation. Delivered by the Finance Department staff, it ensured practical expertise. As a result, the CBOs have improved documentation and communication of their activities, enhanced financial transparency and procurement processes, and increased visibility and engagement within the community.

title.narrative: Number of CBOs identified and selected

description.narrative: TAD successfully completed selection of Partnered Community-Based Organizations (CBOs) in the current project. Recognising the significance of choosing organizations that had shown tangible and positive impact during the previous project, TAD implemented a transparent and independent selection mechanism. This entailed engaging the expertise of the Monitoring and Evaluation Department to devise a comprehensive performance evaluation system. The system collated data from various departments, including programme, financial, procurement, and communication, which were then scrutinised to inform the final selection. The evaluation process was carried out electronically, utilising a clear and standardised grading system to uphold objectivity. Upon completing the evaluation process, TAD extended invitations to the directors of the selected organisations to participate in the current project, with responses overwhelmingly positive, reflecting the organisations' enthusiasm and commitment. Subsequently, TAD convened a project kick-off meeting at their office in Mosul, where directors and members of the organisations were briefed on the project's objectives, duration, donors, contracting method, and terms. Detailed discussions were also held on project activities, action plans, financial and programmatic specifications, and anticipated media documentation methods. Currently, TAD is in the process of finalising contracts to be shared with the selected organisations for their review and signing purposes. These proactive measures by TAD underscore their dedication to ensuring the seamless implementation of the project and the sustained commitment of Partnered CBOs. In the beginning of May, after completing the contracting stage and finalising the budget for the projects and activities of the selected CBOs, TAD met with the six CBOs to sign the collaboration agreements that had previously been shared with them via email.

title.narrative: OP1.1: CSO partners have better planning and management capacity to advocate more effectively for women and girls’ rights in their communities.

description.narrative: Enhanced planning and management capacity of partners is a pivotal step towards more impactful advocacy for the rights of women and girls in their communities. By providing partners with strengthened capacity, NPA anticipates more informed and organized activities that address the specific needs and challenges faced by women and girls. Thus, contributing to positive and sustainable changes within the communities we are supporting.

title.narrative: Number of CSO partners’ staff attended Business Management ToT (disaggregated by female/male)

description.narrative: During August 2024, a five-day ToT was provided to the four partners on Business Management and Development. The business management modules covered key areas as follows: Entrepreneurship Foundation, leadership, Marketing Mix, Digital Marketing, marketing strategies, Business plan, Differentiation between small business and micro business, Safeguarding PSEA (Reporting Pathway), Financial Management, Project life cycle, Developing Business Plan, strategic planning. The trainer also reviewed the tools used by NPA partners and developed them accordingly. In addition, a three-day ToT was provided for three partners on Employment and Soft skills. The soft skills modules emphasized communication, teamwork, conflict resolution, Decision making, Negotiation Management, Time Management, Body language and emotional intelligence, which are crucial for building strong interpersonal relationships and creating a positive work environment. The purpose for these training sessions was to build the skill of livelihood officers and other staff of partners to provide similar training sessions to women and girls in targeted communities as part of the economic empowerment for these women and girls.

title.narrative: Number of trainings/ coaching/ mentoring sessions (desegregated by subject and female/male) provided for CSO partners.

description.narrative: During March 2024, a workshop on Visibility Guidelines provided by NPA Communication and Advocacy Consultant to three protection partners. This contributed to coordinating Presence and Visibility Strategies with NPA’s Partners, and other actors. Two other workshops were organised on Time Management and Organising Priorities to Avoid Stress. The workshops were inspired by Leadership Training ToT by Harvard University and Concern Worldwide that the WPE Project Manager participated in. Furthermore, constant support and mentoring was provided to partners, especially as the partners were in the inception face of the programme. The support varied from planning the quarter to develop tools for coordination with various stakeholders. A specific focus was given to the new partner of the programme. During November and December 2024, a workshop by Communications and Advocacy Advisor was provided to partners on success stories, another one about report writing was provided by the programme manager, furthermore the programme manager provided another training on Lessons Learnt to partners. The partners requested to have more refresher training and/or coaching on these topics, thus in December a refresher coaching session was provided to partners on reporting, lessons learnt and success stories writing. During February 2025, a two-day training on Conflict analysis, Conflict Sensitivity and Conflict Transformation was provided for the four partners in Duhok. The training was provided by the programme manager.

title.narrative: OP 3.2: Quality MHPSS support provided for women and girls 15+ who are survivors or at risk of Violence based on inequality between women and men in Dohuk Mosul.

description.narrative: In order to guarantee that survivors and those who are at risk receive knowledgeable and caring care, the MHPSS activities are created to include a wide range of mental health and psychosocial support. The objective is to build emotional well-being and resilience among the targeted demographic by addressing the unique difficulties and traumas related to violence based on inequality between women and men.

title.narrative: Number of women and girls 15+ received MHPSS services.

description.narrative: During the first quarter of the first year, the three protection partners were able to finalize the hiring process of psychologists. The psychologists initiated their work during March and started providing MHPSS services. While there are varied MHPSS services ranging from individual counselling and outdoor wellbeing group activities. The psychologists will facilitate some psychosocial activities when the need arises. For each case received, the psychologists formulate a treatment programme based on the cases’ needs and through observation of the social workers and other team members. Goals and a treatment plan are then identified to achieve personal, social and vocational development of the cases. The treatment plans are tailored to each case, however in general they focus to identify the signs and symptoms of any psychological disorder such as: depressive disorder, conversion disorder, shockwave disorder, etc. as well as medical history and what triggered these disorders, then based on these the psychologist initiates the treatment plan. One of the most common challenges is the lack of awareness of communities about the MHPSS, as any discussion about the psychological matters is considered stigmatizing and the survivors sometimes are scared about their families finding out they are meeting a psychologist, or the survivors don’t want to be referred out of the fear of the community. With that being said, the Yazidi displaced communities are slightly more open to receive the MHPSS counselling compared to the Muslim community in Mosul city.

title.narrative: OP 3.6: Increased advocacy and awareness for implementing Law No.8 of 2021 (Yazidi Female Survivors Law).

description.narrative: NPA and BWOCD had a meeting with IOM to discuss the priorities of the Survivors and what added value can NPA and partners do. The meeting once again gave NPA and partners the assurance that more awareness to survivors and their families is needed especially in Sinjar district, as well connecting survivors with governmental stakeholders to ensure their voices are heard.

title.narrative: Number of workshops and FGD/meetings for survivor regarding the Law No.8 of 2021

description.narrative: During May and June 2024, two workshops were held by PDO for ISIS survivors. During the workshops the survivors discussed what has been done and what can be done to improve the lives of the survivors and implement the Iraqi Law No.8 of 2021 - Yazidi Female Survivors Law All survivors agreed that more awareness is necessary about the implementation of the law and the content of the law, so that the survivors have sufficient knowledge on how to claim their rights and compensation. The survivors agreed that PDO’s approach of engaging survivors with these workshops and empowering them to demand their rights, is the correct methodology to ensure the sustainability of efforts and achievements of better impacts. An eight-day training course was conducted by BWOCD for ISIS survivors in Sinjar. The main goal was to enhance participants' skills to support their recovery and future advocacy efforts. The course included eight structured training sessions: The first two days focused on the Yazidi Women Survivors Law, where participants learned about its key provisions, how to register under the law, and its importance in securing survivors’ rights. The next two days covered advocacy training, teaching participants techniques and strategies to promote the Yazidi Women Survivors Law and defend survivors’ rights. A one-day life skills training session emphasized resilience, emotional well-being, and personal development, helping participants in their holistic recovery. The public speaking training on another day-built participants' confidence to deliver impactful awareness sessions about the challenges Yazidi survivors face. Communication skills were developed during a dedicated day of training, focusing on conveying messages clearly and building rapport during advocacy efforts. Participants also learned about networking and relationship building to strengthen their advocacy work with community leaders and organizations. Finally, a day was dedicated to negotiation skills, equipping participants to navigate sensitive situations effectively.

title.narrative: Number of meetings conducted with relevant stakeholders including the Ministry of Labour and Social Affairs, the Ministry of Migration and Displacement, the Women Committee of the Iraqi Parliament and others to discuss the implementation of the Law No.8 of 2021

description.narrative: During the first year of the programme, as part of the coordination and/or raising awareness about the struggles of survivors and best methodologies to support them, eight meetings were conducted with stakeholders. These meetings were with the NRC, IRC Warjen organization, Survivors Network and Survivors directorate and Progress in Peace and Hope Maker Organization to reach survivors, and with IOM to obtain and distribute publications and informational materials related to the Yazidi Survivors Law. This partnership ensured that survivors had access to accurate and up-to-date guidance on their rights and the legal processes available to them.

title.narrative: Percentage of interviewed Yazidi female survivors who report they have more awareness about the content and methods to request the compensation entitled for them by the law No. 8.
OP 3.3: Strengthened well-being of women and girls 15+ through community based psychosocial support, grass root advocacy, life skills, and recreational activities:

description.narrative: NPA and partners adopt a holistic approach to enhancing the well-being of women and girls. It involves a multifaceted strategy that incorporates community-based psychosocial support, grassroots advocacy, vocational training, and recreational activities. The aim is to create a supportive community environment that addresses the psychological, social, and recreational needs of women and girls. Through community-based psychosocial support, women and girls will have access to resources and services that promote mental and emotional health. Grassroots advocacy efforts aim to challenge societal norms and stereotypes, contributing to a more inclusive and supportive community.

title.narrative: Number of advocacy initiatives carried out by women and girls 15+ from the supported communities.

description.narrative: Since the beginning of the programme, five grass-root advocacy initiatives were carried out by women and girls in targeted communities. The initiatives that were carried out were: Supporting Women and Girls in Orphanages and Elderly Homes in Mosul city; This campaign aimed to improve living conditions by organizing activities like tree planting and garden clean-ups, providing much-needed emotional support. Second one was Integrating Women and Girls with Disabilities in Mosul city; This initiative raised awareness about the rights of women and girls with disabilities, working to protect them from sexual exploitation. Two other initiatives were carried out in Shariya town, one was building the advocacy skills of women and girls; one of the PSS beneficiaries developed some materials to train women and girls from her community on advocacy skills within their families to advocate for their rights and needs. The second one was planting trees; launched in July 2024, was led by six girls who, after participating in the advocacy sessions, came up with the idea of planting trees in specific areas of Sharya non-camp. They approached the municipality, conveyed the importance of planting trees for the community and how they protect the environment, and successfully obtained approval for the initiative. The municipality was supportive throughout the planning phase. Due to weather conditions, the group had to wait for a suitable time, and by the end of September, they began the tree-planting process with the support of an engineer from the Sharya municipality. The final one was about cleaning the camp of Bersive 1; 17 girls after finishing the course of the PSS on advocacy, approached the camp management with their plan to clean the camps from waste and to promote a healthier environment. Impressed by their efforts, the camp management called for any other NGO along with them to support the girls. Finally, a day was specified, the girls, the camp management and two other NGOs started cleaning camp campaign.

title.narrative: Percentage of outreached women and girls 15+ attending psychosocial and reintegration activities

description.narrative: The psychosocial and reintegration activities within the programme are crucial components that underpin the effectiveness and impact of the advocacy efforts at grass-roots level. With structured sessions focusing on communication skills, equality between men and women, leadership, advocacy message development, and accountability, women and girls are equipped with the knowledge and skills necessary for effective advocacy initiatives at family and community level. These activities not only empower women and girls to communicate their experiences and advocate for their rights but also foster a sense of solidarity, empathy and collective action.

title.narrative: Percentage of women and girls 15+ who regularly (more than 3 times) participated in a recreational, life skills activity.

OP 2.3: CBOs and CSOs, community representatives, local authorities and other stakeholders contribute to developing effective and contextually localized plans of intervention and implementing interventions conducive to prevention of violent extremism and stabilisation.

description.narrative: The TAD programme and MEAL team have created an online form and advertised a call for interest post on their social media account for community members who are willing to participate in the RSCs voluntary opportunity in the six areas of the project.TAD received a total of 508 applications (393 male and 115 female) from individuals who have filled in their information to be part of the RSCs in their areas. After the application period ended, TAD formed a selection committee to analyse the data they received and select the RSC members.TAD selected 24 community members (15 male and nine female), with four representatives from each of the six targeted areas, and signed a code of conduct to establish an official committee. These selected individuals were then introduced to the community and local authorities. Additionally, TAD hired an external international expert to empower RSCs through capacity building trainings on preventing violent extremism (PVE) and to develop, design, and implement effective community initiatives.CBOs programme staff have improved their PVE awareness, designing community initiatives and the analysis of the threats in the areas that operating in that aiming to reduce the level of violence and responding to the PVE indicators that were determined in the community consultation conducted by the CBOs and the RSCs in the targeted areas.The technical and operational capabilities of TAD and the six CBO were enhanced through the review and adaptation of the PVE toolkit and EWS guide. A report template on Early Warning Mechanism indicators was developed to support community awareness campaigns, foster partnerships with stakeholders, and aid in creating PVE-responsive monitoring and evaluation tools. These efforts aim to enable NPA and its partners to deliver comprehensive PVE reintegration and engagement, promoting resilience and preventing violent extremism within Ninewa communities.

title.narrative: Number of community members capacitated and empowered through trainings to establish Resilient and Stabilisation Committees (RSCs), the selected community members will be inclusive and representative i.e., including women.

description.narrative: A committee consisting of the MEAL Officer, Project Manager, and Project Coordinators from TAD was formed to develop a mechanism for including target groups in a way that positively reflects the project and future interventions. This mechanism involved creating selection criteria for community members to be capacitated and engaged with the programme to implement community initiatives. The criteria were inclusive and representative, with special consideration given to vulnerable social groups such as women, youth, minorities, IDPs, and Persons with Disabilities (PwD). The TAD Programme and MEAL team created an online form and advertised a call for interest on their social media account for community members willing to volunteer for RSCs in the six areas of the project. The form included detailed questions covering various aspects such as educational level, participation in civil society, and knowledge related to preventing violent extremism, allowing for the fair and transparent selection of community members. The application forms were announced and disseminated via social media, distributed to partner organisations for further dissemination within their communities, and shared within various working groups and with heads of administrative units in those areas. This ensured that community members who met the criteria could apply to engage with the programme and implement effective community initiatives. TAD received a total of 508 applications (393 men and 115 women) from individuals interested in joining the RSCs in their areas. Following the application period, TAD formed a selection committee to analyse the data received and select the RSC members. To provide the selected RSCs with the tools to prevent violent extremism and promote stability, a training was conducted to the RSCs members. This training utilised a practical, hands-on approach, focusing on applying key frameworks. Participants learnt to analyse their initiatives through a SWOT analysis, establish clear and achievable goals using SMART criteria, and manage the initiatives effectively through a comprehensive lifecycle approach. Additionally, the training equipped the RSCs with problem-solving skills through the problem tree exercise and stakeholder analysis, enabling them to navigate their relationships and develop strategies for collaboration and resistance management. This training empowers community leaders and RSCs to design and implement impactful initiatives, ultimately fostering a more stable and peaceful environment.

title.narrative: Number of people attended capacity building workshops on PVE, and developing, designing, and implementing effective community initiatives

description.narrative: In November 2024, a three-day workshop titled “PVE Toolkit and Early Warning System Guide for NPA CSOs and CBOs" was held in Erbil. TAD organised the workshop, and the NPA PVE consultant facilitated it. This workshop brought together representatives from TAD, CBOs, and sub-national countering violence and extremism in Ninewa to learn about tools and strategies for Preventing Violent Extremism (PVE). The training focused on using the PVE Toolkit and Early Warning System Guide to help CBOs address risks and respond to threats. Participants engaged in discussions, practical exercises, and shared experiences to develop effective ways to prevent violence and strengthen their work in their communities. Additionally, a report template on Early Warning Mechanism indicators was developed to support community awareness campaigns, foster partnerships with stakeholders, and aid in the creation of PVE-responsive monitoring and evaluation tools. The workshop empowered the attendees' skills to evaluate risks and enhance community resilience, aiming to reduce violence and address PVE indicators identified during community consultations conducted after the workshop. The active involvement of community members fostered trust and ownership, leading to sustainable and impactful interventions. A total of 20 participants attended this training (12 men and 8 women).

title.narrative: Number of conferences conducted to ensure community and local authority by-in and explore ways forward in terms of sustainability and entry-points for future interventions

OP 2.2: Strengthened CBOs advocate for community-prioritized needs and challenges

description.narrative: The community consultations resulted in greater engagement, the emergence of new stakeholders and leaders, and a broader awareness of issues. Enhanced collaboration and the identification of overlapping issues highlighted the need for coordinated interventions. In response to the issues raised, some immediate actions were taken by local authorities and organisations.Community consultation sessions strengthened local engagement, broadened stakeholder participation, and increased awareness of key issues affecting community stability. The process enhanced collaboration, surfaced overlapping concerns, and led to immediate actions by local actors. CBOs applied their training in PVE and early warning systems to identify violent extremism indicators, generating actionable data that informed the Early Warning Mechanism. These efforts fostered community ownership and laid the groundwork for coordinated responses and future community-led interventions. CBO and RSC members in Ninewa enhanced their capacity to detect and respond to early signs of violent extremism through standardised assessment and reporting tools. As a result of localised analyses and collaborative review, a refined set of context-specific indicators was developed to guide future interventions. This outcome laid the foundation for more targeted, evidence-based community responses aimed at reducing risk and improving local stability. Through inclusive community consultations, local communities and stakeholders in conflict-affected areas of Ninewa identified critical gaps in essential services, infrastructure, livelihoods, and social inclusion. Practical recommendations were developed to inform future programming and guide more targeted, locally relevant interventions. By actively engaging community influencers and social media activists, CBOs contributed to strengthening community resilience and ensuring that program activities remained responsive to evolving community priorities.

title.narrative: Number of reports developed by NPA CSO on any rise or fall with respect to the Early Warning Mechanism indicators.

description.narrative: Following a comprehensive training facilitated by the NPA PVE Consultant on Preventing Violent Extremism Toolkit and Early Warning System Guide, and the identification of violent extremism indicators, staff from the six CBOs and members of the Resilience and Stabilisation Committees (RSCs) were equipped with the skills needed to detect threats that could undermine community stability in Ninewa. Participants were provided with a standardised reporting template to guide their assessments, enabling consistent and structured analysis across different communities. Using this tool, the CBOs conducted localised assessments and submitted detailed reports highlighting key indicators of violent extremism. A total of 12 reports were produced by the CBOs and RSCs, and further developed by the NPA PVE Consultant. These reports were then reviewed and analysed collaboratively by NPA and TAD to assess trends in the rise or fall of risk levels in relation to the Early Warning Mechanism. The reports drew on a combination of input from stabilisation committees, feedback from community members, and the CBOs' contextual understanding of their operating environments. The goal of this process was the identification of a refined set of violent extremism indicators that now serve as a strategic framework to guide future community-based interventions. These indicators will inform the design and implementation of targeted initiatives that aim to mitigate risks early and strengthen local resilience against radicalisation. The indicators will be monitored and then rise and fall reports will be developed on accordingly.

title.narrative: Number of community consultation sessions conducted by CBOs to elicit qualitative and quantitative data and update the PVE index of the Early Warning Mechanism.

description.narrative: In December 2024, CBOs organized community consultation sessions with local representatives selected to form the Resilience and Stabilisation Committees (RSC). These sessions aimed to engage communities and stakeholders in identifying violent extremism indicators to be integrated into the existing Early Warning Mechanism tool. A total of 120 participants attended six sessions, including 68 men and 52 women.The sessions took place in six targeted areas, with one session held in each area. The primary goal was to involve local communities in identifying and prioritizing indicators of violent extremism. This participatory approach ensured that the Early Warning Mechanism tool was informed by local insights and experiences, enhancing its relevance and effectiveness.Building on this foundation, CBOs applied their training from the PVE Toolkit and Early Warning System as they began the consultation sessions. The outputs from these sessions were indicators of violent extremism in their areas. Organizations will respond to these indicators by coordinating with responders (government or community) or through community initiatives that will be implemented in the upcoming phases of the project.These community consultation sessions not only provided valuable data for the Early Warning Mechanism tool but also strengthened the relationship between CBOs and local communities. The active participation of community members fostered trust and a sense of ownership over the PVE efforts, ultimately contributing to more sustainable and impactful interventions.In February 2025, six local CBOs held six consultation sessions to enhance stabilisation and prevent violent extremism in conflict-affected communities. These sessions allowed participants, who were community representatives, to review and discuss the early warning indicators developed by the NPA PVE consultant, designed to help recognise early signs of radicalisation and violent extremism. These indicators served as a reference framework to guide the evaluation of community risk levels and the shaping of relevant interventions. Each session involved about 20 participants, totalling 125 (46 women, 79 men), including RSC members, local government representatives, and community members such as civil society activists, academics, community leaders, youth, women, and persons with disabilities. Participants discussed early warning indicators of radicalisation, reassessed risk factors, and identified new prevention initiatives. Common challenges identified across locations included social and economic exclusion (such as unemployment and poverty), poor access to basic services (healthcare, electricity, water), the growing influence of online radicalisation and hate speech, intercommunal tensions in post-ISIS areas, and the manipulation of cultural and religious narratives. Building on these findings, participants proposed several community initiatives that could respond to those indicators. These included youth-led campaigns to prevent hate speech, interfaith and intercultural dialogue circles, civic education in schools, media content that promotes coexistence, and legal and documentation support for women to strengthen their civic participation.

title.narrative: Number of community consultation sessions conducted by CBOs with local community representatives.

description.narrative: TAD supervised partnered CBOs to conduct six community consultations and sensitisation sessions in the six locations of the project in Ninewa. Each session aimed to engage local communities and stakeholders in identifying and prioritising community needs and challenges related to basic infrastructure and essential services. A total of 120 participants attended these sessions. In Al-Shoura District, Mosul, on 15 July 2024, 20 participants (eight women and 12 men) gathered to discuss key issues. They identified a lack of staff in schools, leading to overcrowded classrooms, low educational standards, and high dropout rates. Additionally, many children lacked identification documents, hindering their education and causing feelings of exclusion. The Al-Shoura Health Centre faced a shortage of medical equipment and specialist doctors, and farmers in the district struggled with insufficient government support, resulting in low living standards and high unemployment. Proposed solutions included recruiting and retaining more teachers, facilitating the issuance of identification documents, increasing medical equipment and specialist doctors, and developing training programmes for farmers. On 11 July 2024, in Hammam Al-Alil District, 20 participants (eight women and 12 men) addressed issues such as excessive livestock and stray dogs in residential areas, neglect of public funds, lack of job opportunities, and the need for support for vulnerable families. Proposed solutions involved conducting awareness sessions for livestock owners, raising awareness through campaigns, setting up a market for local artisans and craftsmen to showcase and sell their products, and providing school supplies to children from vulnerable families. In Sinjar District, on 24 July 2024, 20 participants (six women and 14 men) discussed judiciary instability due to political conflicts, lack of a dedicated building for Sinjar General Hospital, agricultural challenges, and education shortages. They proposed forming an administration to release financial allocations, allocating land and funds for a new hospital building, providing state support through affordable agricultural inputs, and rehabilitating damaged schools while building new ones. On 18 July 2024, in Al-Ayadhiyah District, 20 participants (eight women and 12 men) identified issues such as the lack of a maternity room, scarcity of treatments for chronic diseases, lack of laboratory equipment, and unemployment of widows and divorcees. Proposed solutions included assigning staff to the maternity room at least two days a week, providing health cards for low-income individuals, acquiring essential laboratory equipment, and offering sewing machines or vocational training for widows and divorcees. In Qayrawan District, on 22 July 2024, 22 participants (seven women and 13 men) highlighted conflicts between farmers and the North Oil Company, lack of school buildings due to land ownership issues, loss of identification documents complicating school enrolment, and motorcycle-related traffic accidents. Proposed solutions were to let farmers use their land for growing crops and grazing animals, facilitate land transfer procedures for school construction, coordinate the issuance of identification documents for children, and ban unlicensed motorcycles while ensuring compliance with safety standards. Finally, in Qayyarah District, on 14 July 2024, 20 participants (eight women and 12 men) discussed air pollution from a nearby sanitary landfill, problems with the Angolan Company seizing agricultural lands, obstacles in receiving benefits and rights for martyrs’ families, and water pollution from sewage in the Tigris River. Proposed solutions included relocating the landfill site, compensating affected farmers, simplifying procedures for martyrs’ families to receive benefits, and developing sewage infrastructure to prevent contamination of the river.

title.narrative: Number of dialogues and consultation meetings conducted by the CBOs to advocate for community needs and challenges, desegregated by location and type.

description.narrative: The Six CBOs partnered with TAD have organised a series of community consultations and awareness sessions during January and February across key areas of the project in Nenewa, including Sinjar, Al-Qayyarah, Hamam Al-Alil, Al-Shura, and Al-Ayadiyah. The purpose was to give space for local communities and stakeholders to openly discuss and priorities their pressing needs, particularly regarding essential services and infrastructure. Each session, involving around 20 to 25 participants, was carefully structured to ensure the meaningful participation of women and youth. To guarantee broad representation, the CBOs collaborated with local councils and networks to invite a diverse mix of stakeholders, including government officials, service providers, community leaders, civil society activists, returnees, youth, and people with disabilities. Participatory tools, such as group discussions and problem analysis exercises, were used to explore the root causes of local challenges and to identify practical solutions. As the sessions progressed, five major themes consistently emerged: the lack of healthcare facilities and medical staff; overcrowded or damaged schools and transportation challenges; poor infrastructure, unreliable electricity and water services, and outdated sanitation systems; high unemployment rates among youth and women; and limited access to psychosocial support and social inclusion for marginalized groups. Participants proposed actionable solutions such as building and equipping hospitals, renovating schools, repairing infrastructure, establishing vocational training and small business programs, and providing mental health and inclusion services. Local leaders actively engaged in the discussions, and women and youth expressed strong interest in taking more active roles in decision-making processes. Despite facing challenges such as cultural barriers to women's participation, logistical difficulties in remote areas, and occasional absences of government officials due to scheduling conflicts, the CBOs successfully adapted by organising separate sessions and overcoming planning hurdles. Following the completion of the sessions, the CBOs conducted a thorough analysis of the findings, categorising needs and priorities for each location. The results are now being prepared for presentation to local and national decision-makers to inform future programming, planning, and advocacy efforts. In total, across the eleven sessions held, there were 121 male and 89 female participants, reflecting a strong level of community engagement and a significant step toward promoting inclusive development and resilience within conflict-affected areas.

title.narrative: Number of coordination meetings conducted to increase synergies to mutually contribute to updating and enhancing the National Strategy to Combat Extremism Conducive to Terrorism and endorsing the Early Warning System for south and west Ninewa

Number of update reports developed by CSO partner at Ninewa’s Peace and Reconciliation Working Group to provide early warning signals to the working groups members, which include international donors, international agencies, international NGOs, and local NGOs.

Number of result-based dialogue sessions engaging the key local authority stakeholders to advocate for community needs and challenges identified and prioritised through the community sessions conducted.
OP 3.7: Outreach and awareness sessions conducted for community members in the targeted locations of Duhok and Mosul on women and girls’ well-being and empowerment.

description.narrative: The outreach efforts seek to raise awareness of the specific challenges and opportunities experienced by women and girls within their communities, as well as to spread useful information and foster understanding of women’s rights and potentials. The sessions aim to promote positive attitudes, support networks, and insights that help to the overall improvement of the lives and rights of women and girls in the targeted locations. The sessions address violence based on inequality of men and women and ways to combat the violence by encouraging community members to increase their awareness and understanding.

title.narrative: Number of community members outreached and attended awareness sessions on women and girls’ well-being and empowerment

description.narrative: During the reporting period, partners provided awareness sessions on topics such as early marriage and its consequences, strengthening communication skills for women and girls who are students or are in the workforce, online harassment, domestic violence, problem solving skills, and stress management and online abuse. On of the issues reported in Mosul city center was lack of trust and questioning by people about the goal and mission of the NGOs operating in their areas. NPA partner in Mosul, BWOCD, faced constant scrutiny from the people in the neighbourhoods they are targeting, thus it was necessary to adress this issue and assure people that the aim is humanitarian. BWOCD focused on raising awareness about their work and their mission in the area. Moreover, NPA provided a training to all BWOCD field staff on Communication with Communities and Do No Harm as well as Safeguarding, to ensure the staff are safe and have clear messages when communicating with targeted areas communities. Apart from that, BWOCD had to halt their activities in one of the neighbourhoods due to tribal tensions that increased and caused security concerns.

title.narrative: OP 1.3: CSO partners have improved capacity to deliver quality services to conflict-affected women and girls 15+, including case management to survivors, PSS to women, men, girls and boys 15+, and women's rights and equality between men and women.

description.narrative: The planned capacity development activities will make use of the existing knowledge and skills that partners have acquired in previous years. Before the start of each capacity development training, an assessment will be conducted to evaluate the partners' current level of knowledge. Following that, training materials will be tailored to address specific needs identified in the assessment. In order to ensure sustainability and foster knowledge sharing, each partner will formulate a comprehensive plan outlining how they intend to share knowledge and effectively apply the obtained skills in their respective contexts. This approach aims to enhance the long-term impact of the capacity development efforts and promote a culture of ongoing learning and collaboration among the partners.

title.narrative: Number of CSO staff attended technical training and workshops on topics of Core Concepts violence based on inequality between women and men, Human Right Equality, Outreach, Case Management, MHPSS, Life-Skills and Self-Care, Advocacy, Information Management System of violence reports, Awareness Raising, etc.

description.narrative: In April and May, NPA Iraq and partners participated in capacity development sessions provided by the HO Equality Advisor, which included NPA's Equality Policy, Equality Programming in the PMC, and Equality Mainstreaming in MEAL. A workshop on the 2024 Joint Iraq Implementation Plan for NPA’s Equality Policy, integrating Equality responsive and transformative approaches in Iraq’s 2024-2028 Strategy, the Rapid Equality Analysis (RGA) Tool, equality and inclusion in NPA’s programming (diversity, disability, youth, and minority groups).

title.narrative: Number of CSO partners with confidential case management documentation systems ranking ‘good’.

description.narrative: The three partners of protection have all finalized setting up a confidential case management documentation system based on the standardized information management system. Assessing the level of satisfaction of the documentation system is done through constant follow up by NPA and by the Scorecard Assessment; that is usually conducted in year two or after year two of the programme.

title.narrative: Number of CSO partners who have at least 3 staff/volunteers who can facilitate life skills and psychosocial sessions.

description.narrative: The three partners of protection have trained staff/volunteers to facilitate the life skills sessions. All partners’ staff are trained on facilitation techniques, each partner has assigned one staff to become a focal point for one or more activities, and that staff is responsible for sharing knowledge, training new staff and updating the team on any changes. The staff and volunteers on the field also have regular meetings to make sure they all are aware of the changes in the context and/or behaviours of the communities, thus responding directly to any surging change. During March 2025, a training was provided to BWOCD field staff in Mosul city, regarding Communication with Communities, Do No Harm, Safeguarding and facilitation techniques. The training aimed at increasing the awareness of staff on safe communication with targeted communities through outreach and providing other services, especially since the tensions and concerns of population towards NGOs has increased.

title.narrative: Number of CSOs staff trained in case management

description.narrative: NPA not only provides training internally but is constantly searching for capacity development opportunities for partners through coordination with other NGOs in areas of operation. Apart from training partners’ staff, NPA constantly follows up with partners and provides mentoring and on-the-job coaching for the social workers and team leaders. NPA and partners had a meeting in February to discuss the latest context changes and the decision of the Iraqi Parliament to pass the amendments to the Personal Status law No. 188 of 1959. The aim was to examine how this law will affect communities and determine how NPA and partners can adapt to more effectively support women and girls.

title.narrative: OP 3.4: Improved social support and recreational activities are provided for men and boys 15+.

description.narrative: The program recognizes the important role that men and boys play in fostering an inclusive and equitable society. By increasing their awareness, the programme aims to promote a deeper understanding of the challenges faced by women and the importance of achieving equality between men and women. Through tailored masculinity programme, the awareness of men and boys regarding equality will be increased and they will be encouraged to become advocates for women's rights and contribute to dismantling existing disparities. The curricula for the masculinity sessions have been developed, as changes are needed based on the lessons learnt of the prior programme.

title.narrative: Number of men and boys 15+ attended social support and recreational activities, desegregated by location

description.narrative: One of the lessons learnt from the previous programmes is that engaging with men and boys is different than engaging with women and girls. Men and boys have their own needs and requests, for example, during the mornings they are busy working or going to school, thus the partners consult with them before planning any activity. Men and boys also are less interested in awareness sessions thus any activity that is targeted towards them should have some recreational and entertainment aspects. Apart from that men and boys are often not the targeted groups for NGOs, thus they feel left out. Encouraging them to participate in social activities leads to better reflection on social norms from their sides thus increasing their willingness to become allies for women's rights.

title.narrative: OP 4.1: Improved economic skills for conflict affected women through vocational trainings and business management skills development.

description.narrative: The programme aims to empower women by providing them with practical knowledge and expertise relevant to improbity skills, as well as small business operations. Business management skills development will focus on entrepreneurial skills such as financial literacy, market understanding, marketing of products and services and strategic planning. By improving economic skills through these targeted efforts, the project aims to enable women to establish and manage small businesses effectively, fostering economic independence and resilience for women and their families.

title.narrative: Number of soft and employable skills trainings conducted, desegregated by type of training

description.narrative: During March 2024, one training course for young men and women that extended for six days was provided by PDO in coordination with Hevi Volunteer group and DCVAW on how to build skills and enhance the capabilities of new graduates to enable them to obtain and reach the necessary resources that enable them to rely completely on themselves and develop their mental, psychological and physical capabilities. It is worth noting that the course covered more than one different topic by professional trainers, including journalists, some of them who work in the government, as well as lawyers and trainers in the field of self-development. During the last quarter of the first year, three soft and employable skills training sessions were provided for the newly graduates and other women looking to get into the workforce. The main topics discussed were Self-esteem, Emotional management, Creativity Decision making and problem solving, Effective communication, Negotiation, Teamwork, Time and stress management. As well as good practices for C.V. writing and interview skills. The training session took place in Duhok and Ninewa.

title.narrative: Number of business mentoring, networking and coaching sessions provided to women

description.narrative: During the first year of the programme, two networking sessions were organized by partners for 28 business owners, where new established business owners met with the already existing businesses and received advice from them but also increased coordination with each other in terms of work collaborations and/or client referrals.

title.narrative: Number of women attended business and management skills, desegregated by type of training.

description.narrative: The partners' livelihood officers, who received training from the Business Management consultant, created their own training materials with the consultant's support. They then conducted Business and Management skills training sessions for women and girls in the targeted locations. These women and girls were selected to receive small grants to start their own businesses. These training sessions not only improve the financial independence of women and girls but also boost their self-esteem, empowering them to stand up for their rights and avoid abusive situations. By entering the business world, these women challenge traditional gender roles, support gender equality, and promote their leadership in the community.

title.narrative: OP 4.2: Established and strengthened micro-enterprises of conflict affected women.

description.narrative: The programme aims to empower women to establish and sustain small businesses that serve as a source of income and economic stability for them and their families. By establishing and strengthening small businesses, the programme seeks to enhance the economic empowerment and self-reliance of women in conflict-affected communities, ultimately fostering long-term socio-economic development and empowerment.

title.narrative: Number of new women supported with micro-enterprises

description.narrative: During April and May 2024, the Livelihood Officer started the process of gathering curriculum vitae and coordinated with Social Workers, diverse sectors, organisations, and Camp Management in targeted areas to identify qualified women who were interested in establishing their own businesses or growing their current ones. During the first year of the programme, the partners were able to support 66 women to start their own businesses based on the business ideas these women selected. During the reporting period, partners have identified women needing support to start their businesses and started the process by giving them trainings necessary, helping them develop their business plans and providing the financial support.

title.narrative: Number of previously supported women received additional support in terms of materials or grants, desegregated by type of support provided

description.narrative: During March 2024, the Livelihood Officers of the partners set plans to follow-up with the existing businesses and assess their needs. After an extensive assessment by the Livelihood Officers, ten already existing businesses received additional support. Before choosing these businesses a set of criteria were developed and interviews with women took place to see what their plans were in terms of improving or expanding their existing businesses. During the first year of the programme, partners were able to provide additional support to the 22 women who were supported before. These women were selected based on criteria developed by NPA and partners to ensure the sustainability and development of their businesses. One of the main criteria was that the business is contributing to elimination of violence based on inequality between women and men.

title.narrative: Total amount of USD grants provided to women for their micro-enterprises, desegregated by cases (old and new)
OP 3.1: Quality case management and referral services provided for women and girls 15+ who are at risk or survivors of Violence based on inequality between women and men .

description.narrative: This output is dedicated to strengthening the support services for women and girls 15+, who have experienced the impact of conflict accompanied by the violence based on inequality between men and women. The aim is to provide a tailored and holistic approach towards the recovery and reintegration of these women and girls. The programme focuses on delivering tailored case management services, ensuring that each survivor receives support that is aligned with her unique needs. This approach aims to empower women and girls to regain agency and control over their lives. Additionally, the programme emphasizes the importance of referrals to specialised services, ranging from medical and legal support to MHPSS and governmental support. By facilitating connectionto these vital services, the programme seeks to address the multifaceted needs of survivors and contribute to their holistic recovery. Continuous support is at the core of this programme, as reflected in the follow-up calls provided to survivors who receive referrals. Lastly, the programme recognizes the significance of meeting immediate and urgent needs, offering simple services such as in-kind support and non-food items as well as other needs that might arise and need to be dressed urgently. This approach contributes to theoverall well-being of survivors and contributes to their empowerment and resilience.

title.narrative: Percentage of cases receiving referrals that have received a follow up call within one week after referral.

description.narrative: During the reporting period, 17 cases were refereed to different service providers. While survivors require various case management services, the program efficiently addresses many of these needs. However, there are instances where survivors may need specialized services. In such cases, social workers play a crucial role by referring survivors to the available specialized services. The referral process is particularly important given the reduction of services in multiple locations, especially the camps in KRI. NPA and partners actively coordinate with existing service providers and other stakeholders to comprehensively map out available services and stay updated on the latest available services.

title.narrative: Percentage of cases receiving referrals to specialized services (medical, child protection, legal, education, livelihood etc).

description.narrative: Since the beginning of the programme 112 cases were referred to different service providers. While survivors require various case management services, the program efficiently addresses many of these needs. However, there are instances where survivors may need specialized services. In such cases, social workers play a crucial role by referring survivors to the available specialized services. The referral process is particularly important given the reduction of services in multiple locations, especially the camps in KRI. NPA and partners actively coordinate with existing service providers and other stakeholders to comprehensively map out available services and stay updated on the latest available services.

title.narrative: Number of women and girls 15+ received case management services.

description.narrative: Since the beginning of the programme 625 new cases were received, these women and girls experienced different types of violence based on inequality between men and women ranging from physical assault, emotional abuse, denial of resources and early marriage. It is worth mentioning that emotional abuse and denial of resources remain the most prevalent forms of violence based on inequality between men and women, as women still struggle to receive their rights, and the patriarchal beliefs restrict their freedom to have access to resources or to be in equal footstep as men.

title.narrative: Number of women and girls receiving simple needs (in-kind, NFI, etc.) services

description.narrative: The Social Workers of CSO partners analyse the needs of each survivor along with the survivor herself, these needs and the actions to address them are recorded; and the Social Workers take on the task to make sure these needs are met. Apart from the need for MHPSS, medical and legal services, the need for immediate food or NFI is still apparent. Since the beggining of the programme 232 survivors benefited from simple needs, of which most received food items, other categories included; medicines, hygiene kits and clothes.

title.narrative: OP1.2: CSO partners have better organizational capacity (e.g., project management, Human Resources, MEAL, Logistics and Procurement, Security and Financial Management capacities).
Percentage improvement in the capacity level of CSO partners who have demonstrated improved HR, MEAL, logistics, finance and planning capacity, ranking ‘satisfactory’ in an NPA capacity assessments.

description.narrative: A training on Finance Management was provided to the partners, A five-day ToT was provided to four partners on Business Management and Development in Duhok. In total 12 participants benefited from this training. The training focused on the Fundamentals of Using Cash and Accrual Basis, Preparation of Financial Statements and Managing Currency Differences and preparing the budget and trail balance. The training lasted for three days and was held in Duhok. The overall knowledge increase was 14.73% and the feedback of the participants was very positive. NPA continuously provided job coaching, and visits to partners’ implementation sites and HQ to support them in improving their HR, financial management, logistics and security procedures.

title.narrative: Number of CSO partners that have demonstrated improved security management capacity, ranking ‘satisfactory’ in NPA capacity assessment.

description.narrative: Continuing the efforts that NPA with Sida support initiated in February 2023, NPA conducted a three-day Security and Safety Training for all NPA partners in December 2024 (including those under this grant, one security focal point per organization). In total 13 participants (two women and 11 men) and two NPA staff (both male) participated in this training. The aim of this training was to provide NPA’s partners with the necessary skills to identify and analyse security risks in their respective areas of operation, enabling them to effectively handle emergency situations and maintain the safety and security of their staff. The Security and Safety Training was theoretical and practical, and included topics such as: Security principles, security strategies, context analysis, risk analysis, crisis management, and first aid. The overall knowledge increase was 119% and the feedback of the participants was very positive.

title.narrative: Strengthened Civil Society Organisations function more independently and effectively in implementing stability and protection interventions in Iraq.

Number of CSO partners who receive an overall ‘high’ score on NPA’s Organisational Development Dialogue Assessment Tool (ODDAT) [The tool measures the score under five assessment areas: 1. The policy of the organisation; 2. The internal democracy and unity of the organisation; 3. Capacity to influence, have impact and make changes; 4. Capacity to relate to, and make alliances with, other actors; and 5. The technical and administrative competences of the organisation]

description.narrative: In December 2023, NPA conducted the ODDAT for the partners. While all partners showed satisfactory performance across the five key assessment areas, improvement was seen as necessary. Partners showed readiness to enhance their policies, especially in areas where organizational policies might accurately reflect strategic objectives. Moreover, partners will benefit from refining their capacities to increase their influence and effective change. Lastly, the results showed the necessity of enhancing partners’ technical and administrative competencies, ensuring smoother implementation of the programme.

title.narrative: Number of supported CSO partners who joined consortiums/ networks for influencing about Violence based on inequality between women and men and conflict issues in Iraq.

description.narrative: Three of the supported partners are members of different networks and/or consortiums, including: The 188 Alliance (the coalition opposing amendments to the Iraqi Personal Status Law No. 188 of 1959 (PSL)), Kurdistan Women Alliance, Womentum (which focuses on empowering and supporting women organization in MENA region), and the Coalition for Just Reparations (C4JR), among others. Moreover, the partners are active in many groups and meetings such as MHPSS working groups, Camp Management meetings, GBV/women empowerment working groups in Duhok, Ninewa, Erbil, and Suleimani. The partners' strong coordination with each other strengthens their cooperation in terms of applying to new funds as consortium and/or forming coordination to advocate for women rights and equality.

title.narrative: OP 3.5: Stakeholders have better understanding and promote equality between men and women concept and practices, violence based on inequality between women and men core concept and survivor-centred approaches.

Number of people (governmental entities, community/religious leaders, community members, CSOs, activists, media actors, and university students, etc.) capacitated on equality between men and women concept and practices, Violence based on inequality between women and men core concept and survivor-centred approach service provision.

description.narrative: Since the beginning of the programme 60 individuals from various stakeholders in Duhok were capacitated on equality between men and women concept and best practices. The training sessions aimed to enhance understanding and promote the concept of gender equality and its practices, as well as eliminating misconceptions of feminism was discussed by Emma with their training participants. It focused on increasing awareness of gender equality concepts, SGBV core principles, and respectful engagement with SGBV survivors seeking services from stakeholders. By enhancing the capacity, knowledge, and awareness of the participants, the training sought to foster a more equitable environment. All participants had more than three years working experience, however a considerable number of them expressed that this is the first time they have participated in a training like this, especially those who were working in the education or journalism sector. While NGOs and other actors were very active over the last 10 years in providing essential capacity building to the stakeholders, it was noticed that these efforts have been reduced due to decrease in the number of NGOs in Duhok governorate. A concern previously raised by NPA partners, that there are many new faces working with actors that are involved directly or indirectly in SGBV prevention and response. These new individuals need more comprehensive training sessions especially on how to work with survivors in a sensitive and respectful manner.

title.narrative: Number of forums conducted to discuss the key areas towards women protection and empowerment, as well as survivor-centred approach service provision.
OP 1.5: CSO partners are strengthened to become active actors in facilitating, mobilizing, and empowering their communities to become more stable.

Number of CSO partners’ staff attended training courses on PVE toolkit, enhancing their understanding of the drivers of violent extremism and equipping them with tools and strategies to prevent and counteract its spread within their communities.
Number of discussions/ meetings conducted with NPA CSO partners to develop plans, PVE materials, community initiatives, etc.
OP 1.4: CSO partners’ Women Community Centres and satellite safe spaces are functional for confidential counselling and indoor recreation and continue operating in the selected areas.
Number of mobile spaces that are equipped by partners to conduct activities in the camps and non-camp areas.

description.narrative: Emma, PDO and BWO have three static centres open and functioning. Apart from that Emma and PDO have six mobile spaces, one is a rented centre in Sharya town and five are spaces received from camp management to conduct activities in the camps of Kabarto, Qadia, Chammishko, Bajid Kandala, and Bersive. There used to be two Bersive camps, however the two camps are now merged in one, which means that in order to cover the big camp apart from receiving the space, Emma needs to conduct door to door activities as part of outreach; as well as for those families that are far from the centre. This is the same approach that PDO adopted to cover Kabarto 1, Kabarto 2 and Chammishko camp, which is one of the biggest IDPs camps in Iraq. Given that the services are reducing in camps while some other camps have no case management services at all, partners often find themselves overwhelmed with cases referred to them. Apart from that many NGOs have reported during meetings that the domestic violence has increased as a result of the camp closure news, because many families had disagreements among themselves leading to physical violence sometimes. During November 2024, BWOCD opened a mobile space in Sinjar to facilitate the implementation of activities for the ISIS survivors in Sinjar.

title.narrative: Number of Women’s Community Centres that are fully furnished, equipped, staffed and operational by the third Quarter of the project.

description.narrative: Three community centres were established and are fully furnished, one in Khanke town managed by PDO, one in Duhok city managed by Emma and one in Mosul managed by BWOCD. The new partner of the programme (BWOCD) ensured that after the establishment of the community centre in Mosul. The communities were informed about the importance of the services provided, and how these services can benefit the whole communities.

% survivors who received case management services rank their overall satisfaction with the quality of case management services as 4 or 5 out of 5. (Confidential, respectful, supportive, helpful advice, referral access, and timely follow-up).

description.narrative: The survivors are usually met during or at the closure stage of case management to see their satisfaction and whether there are areas that partners can develop. All interviews are done with utmost confidentiality and with informed consent of the survivor. During the first year of the programme, the satisfaction was 100% by survivors (44% ranked their satisfaction 4 and 56% ranked their satisfaction 5), they attributed this satisfaction to the good listening skills of the social workers, the care and empathy they received as well as the constant follow up and referral. NPA and partners will ensure this positive feedback from survivors will continue and that the needs of survivors will always be met with care and respect. The satisfaction of the survivors till the time of the reporting is 97%, most survivors attribute this to the respect shown to them, their needs that were met and how their conditions improved exponentiality after receiving the case management. However, one trend that partners noticed due to the US-funding freeze is the fact that in most camps the partners are now the only service providers, which adds to the pressure of reduced services.

title.narrative: % of women, men, girls and boys 15+ who demonstrate an improved Equality between men and women Indicator score.
